“No angle of head-up tilt over a two-hour duration was associated with any change in forearm and hand volume”.
the effect of two-hour head-up tilt on forearm and hand volumes was not significant in asymptomatic subjects.
the angle of head-up tilt does not affect forearm and/or hand volume.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of body tilt on arm volume and the effect on arm volume of two hours in head-up tilt at 8, 10 and 14 degrees.
the effects of head-up tilt on arm volume.
the effect of body posture on upper limb volume.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of gravity on arm volume are not significant.
the effect of gravity on upper limb volume is minimal and therefore the efficacy of a proposed treatment for upper limb oedema in the supine position is unlikely to be effective.
the effects of two hours of lying at three different angles of head-up on forearm volume were not statistically significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no evidence that a simple intervention of head-up tilt at three different angles of 8 degrees, 11 degrees, and 14 degrees over a two-hour duration is effective in reducing upper limb volume.
there is no significant difference in upper limb volume between the supine position and any of the three angles of head-up lying.
the effect of gravity is not sufficient to reduce upper limb volume.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of body positioning on upper limb volume is not well established.
there is no significant difference in arm volume between lying flat and lying up at different angles.
the use of gravity to reduce arm volume is not an appropriate strategy.
